title: How to Thaw a Turkey Safely
subtitle: Fridge, Cold Water or Frozen
intro: Running late on the Thanksgiving bird? A turkey can be thawed safely three ways: in the refrigerator, in cold water, or not at all. These steps follow USDA food safety guidance, rewritten in plain words so the bird stays out of the temperature danger zone.
desc: How to thaw a turkey safely for Thanksgiving: never on the counter, about one day in the fridge per 4-5 pounds, or 30 minutes per pound in cold water changed every half hour. Short on time? Cook it from frozen and check 165°F in the thigh. Full list on the blog.

title: Old-Time Crock Sauerkraut
subtitle: Grandma's Cabbage Ferment
items: Toss if slimy or smells off
intro: Long before freezers, farm families put up the fall cabbage crop as sauerkraut in a stoneware crock. Salt draws out the juice, and the cabbage ferments under its own brine. Here is the old method in our own words, with the salt ratio and temperatures from the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning.
desc: Old-time crock sauerkraut the way farm families made it: shred firm cabbage, mix 3 tablespoons canning salt per 5 pounds, pack it under its own brine, weigh it down and ferment 3-4 weeks at 70-75°F. Old-fashioned food preservation for the winter pantry. Full list on the blog.

title: Grow Lights for Seedlings 101
subtitle: Stocky Starts, Not Leggy Ones
items: Hang lights close to the tops
Put the lights on a timer
desc: Grow lights for seedlings, a beginner's guide: hang lights close to the plant tops, run them 14-16 hours a day on a timer, raise them as seedlings grow and use a small fan for sturdy stems before hardening off. See the simple seed-starting setup. (Contains affiliate links.)

title: Row Covers for Winter Greens
subtitle: Keep Harvesting in the Cold
items: Double the cover in deep cold
intro: Kale, spinach, collards and lettuce can keep producing well into winter if you give them a little shelter. A floating row cover over simple hoops traps the ground's warmth at night and blocks drying wind. These are the basics for beginners.
desc: Row covers for winter greens: lay frost cloth over hoops, pin the edges against wind, water before a hard freeze, add a second layer in deep cold and vent on sunny days to keep kale, spinach and lettuce growing in late fall and winter. Full list on the blog.

title: How to Can Apple Juice
subtitle: USDA-Tested Water Bath Method
intro: Fresh cider season is the time to put up apple juice for the winter pantry. Letting the juice settle and straining it gives a clear, good-tasting result. These steps follow the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning for a boiling water bath.
desc: How to can apple juice the USDA-tested way: chill fresh-pressed juice 24-48 hours, pour off the clear part, strain, heat until it begins to boil, fill jars with 1/4-inch headspace and process pints or quarts 5 minutes in a boiling water bath, adjusting for altitude. Full list on the blog.

title: Winter Coop Ventilation Tips
subtitle: Dry Air Means Healthy Hens
items: About 1 sq ft vent per 10 hens
intro: Cold rarely hurts healthy chickens, but damp air does. Hens breathe out a lot of moisture overnight, and in a closed-up coop it settles on combs and wattles and raises the risk of frostbite and respiratory trouble. Good winter ventilation moves that moist air out without blowing on the birds.
desc: Winter coop ventilation for backyard chickens: vent high above the roosts, keep drafts off sleeping hens, plan about 1 square foot of vent per 10 birds, change wet bedding and watch for frost or ammonia. Keep your flock healthy and dry all winter. Full list on the blog.
